lead: Ice on an aircraft destroys lift, adds weight and blinds the sensors that tell the crew their speed and height. Ice protection keeps the critical surfaces clear: hot air or electric heaters stop ice forming, and rubber boots or fluid remove it after it has formed. Rain protection keeps the windscreen clear so the runway stays visible. Most of it is switched, timed and monitored electrically.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for the bleed air that feeds thermal anti-icing.

blocks.text: Most airframe icing happens between 0 °C and about −20 °C in cloud or rain holding supercooled droplets: water still liquid below freezing. A droplet freezes as soon as it hits a surface at or below 0 °C, and wing leading edges, spinners, windscreens and probes are exactly that in flight.

items: Extra weight: a 3 mm layer over 12 m² of wing is 32.4 kg on one side.
Loss of lift: the rough leading edge breaks the smooth airflow, so C<sub>Lmax</sub> falls and drag rises.
Earlier stall: lower C<sub>Lmax</sub> and higher weight both raise the stall speed.
Tailplane: its thinner section and shorter chord make a thin layer a large fraction of the chord, so pitch control can be lost when the flaps go down.
Blind sensors: ice in a pitot head gives a false airspeed, and on a static port a false altitude as well.
Engine and propeller: ice shed into the engine damages blades and can cause a compressor stall; ice on a propeller causes vibration and thrust loss.

blocks.where: V<sub>stall</sub> is the stall speed in m/s; W is the aircraft weight in N, including the ice; ρ is air density in kg/m³; S is wing area in m²; C<sub>Lmax</sub> is the maximum lift coefficient, which falls when the leading edge is rough.

blocks.text: Ice also costs time: after freezing rain the aircraft needs fluid sprayed by a de-icing rig before departure, and the crew checks the fluid's holdover time.

Two words carry most of the marks. Anti-icing prevents ice forming on a surface: the skin is held above 0 °C, or coated with fluid that stops the droplet freezing. De-icing lets ice form and then removes it. One aircraft often uses both: hot air on the wing leading edges and a boot on the tail, or boots on the wing and electric heat on the probes.

head: Method
How it works
Typical use
rows: Hot compressor air runs through piccolo tubes inside the leading edge, keeping the skin above 0 °C, then vents overboard
Wing and tail leading edges, engine inlet lips on transports
Heater wires or mats under the skin or in the glass. Probes and windscreens are heated continuously; propeller and some leading-edge mats are switched in timed cycles between zones to share the power
Pitot and AoA probes, windscreens, propellers, the 787 wing
Glycol seeps through a porous leading edge and lowers the freezing point of the water landing on it
Small aircraft and some business jets; limited by fluid carried
Rubber tubes inflate, the skin stretches, brittle ice cracks off; de-icing only
A coil under the skin drives it out in a fast pulse and shatters the ice

blocks.text: Bleed air is not free. It comes from the engine compressor, so thrust falls and fuel burn rises while anti-icing is on, and the ducting, valves and regulators add weight and maintenance. Electric mats need generator capacity instead, so they suit small areas and short duty cycles.

Pneumatic boots: an older rule told crews to wait for 6 to 13 mm of ice before the first cycle, for fear of ice bridging (a thin layer stretching with the boot and staying on it). Tests on modern boots found bridging very rare, so current guidance for most types is to start the boots at the first sign of ice and keep them cycling on the timer, following the flight manual.

sections.h3: Protected areas, ice detection and rain removal

blocks.text: Protection is fitted where ice does the most harm, not over the whole airframe; weight and cost forbid that.

items: Wing leading edges, and the leading edges of the horizontal and vertical tail.
Engine inlet lips, the spinner and, on turboprops, the propeller blades (electric mats at the root).
Pitot heads, angle of attack vanes and the total air temperature probe, heated electrically; static ports on some types.
Windscreen, heated electrically for both ice and mist.
Water drain masts and lines, so they do not freeze.

blocks.text: Detection can be visual: a wing inspection light lets the crew see ice at night. Automatic ice detectors put a probe in the airstream, often a rod vibrating at a set frequency that falls as ice mass builds; at a set drop the detector lights an ICE annunciator, heats the probe clean and starts again. On some types it switches the anti-icing or boots on directly.

Rain removal works on the windscreen. Wipers are driven by an electric or hydraulic motor, and a spring holds the blade on the glass. Some jets use a rain-removal air curtain, a jet of hot bleed air blown across the screen, and many now rely on a permanent hydrophobic coating that makes water bead and blow away. The windscreen heater has an embedded temperature sensor and a controller that holds the glass warm, often on two power levels, with overheat protection so the layers do not delaminate.

examples.question: A turboprop of mass 20 000 kg has a wing area of 61 m² and a clean C<sub>Lmax</sub> of 1.6 at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²). Ice adds 100 kg and lowers C<sub>Lmax</sub> to 1.25. Find the stall speed before and after, in m/s and knots (1 kt = 0.5144 m/s).
steps: Split the causes: the weight alone gives √(20 100 ÷ 20 000) = 1.0025, a 0.25 % rise; the C<sub>Lmax</sub> loss gives √(1.6 ÷ 1.25) = 1.131, a 13.1 % rise.
examples.answer: The stall speed rises from 111.4 kt to 126.3 kt. Almost all of the rise comes from the lost lift, not from the weight of the ice.

traps: Calling a pneumatic boot anti-icing. It is de-icing: it lets ice form and then cracks it off.
Listing only the wing when asked where protection is fitted. Tailplane, engine inlet, propeller, pitot and static heads, windscreen and drain masts all count.
Writing that boots must always wait for a thick layer. That is old guidance; modern boots are cycled from the first sign of ice unless the flight manual says otherwise.
Blaming the ice weight for the higher stall speed. A few kilograms of ice matter far less than the lost C<sub>Lmax</sub>; and 3 mm is 0.003 m, not 0.03 m, in the mass sum.
Forgetting that bleed-air anti-icing steals compressor air, so thrust falls and fuel burn rises while the system is on.

quiz.a: Anti-icing prevents ice forming, for example by keeping the skin above 0 °C with hot air. De-icing removes ice after it has formed, for example by inflating a rubber boot so the ice cracks off.

quiz.q: Name four areas of an aircraft, other than the wing, that need ice protection.
quiz.a: Any four of: horizontal and vertical tail leading edges, engine inlet lip, propeller blades, pitot head and static port, windscreen, drain masts, air temperature probe.

quiz.q: Why does a rough, iced leading edge raise the stall speed?
quiz.a: Roughness makes the airflow separate earlier, so the maximum lift coefficient C_Lmax falls. In V_stall = √(2W ÷ (ρ S C_Lmax)) a smaller C_Lmax raises the stall speed. The added ice weight raises W, which raises it further.

quiz.q: Why is a thin ice layer on the horizontal tail more dangerous than the same layer on the wing?
quiz.a: The tail has a thinner section and shorter chord, so the same ice thickness is a larger fraction of its chord and spoils its flow sooner. When the flaps go down the tail must make more down-load at a larger negative angle, close to its own stall; if it stalls the nose pitches down at low height.

quiz.q: A 2 mm ice layer forms over 9 m² of tailplane. Ice density is 900 kg/m³. Find the volume and the mass.
A crew in icing cloud sees ice building on the wing boots. Older notes say "wait for half an inch". What should they do today, and why?
quiz.a: Follow the flight manual, which for most modern types says to start the boots at the first sign of ice and keep them cycling. Tests showed ice bridging is very rare on modern boots, while waiting lets a rough layer cut C<sub>Lmax</sub> and raise the stall speed.

quiz.q: Compare bleed-air thermal anti-icing with electro-thermal mats for a twin turboprop on a regional route.
quiz.a: Bleed air protects a large area continuously but takes compressor air, so thrust and fuel burn suffer, and it needs ducts, valves and regulators along the leading edge. Electric mats need no ducting and route easily along a small surface, but they load the generators. A common split on such an aircraft is boots on the wing for de-icing, with electric heat on the propellers, probes and windscreen.

quiz.q: Why is a wiper not the only rain removal method on a fast aircraft?
quiz.a: At high speed the airflow can lift the blade off the glass and the arm loads are large. Heat, an air curtain or a hydrophobic coating clear the screen with no moving arm, so some aircraft rely on those.

beyond: Not for the exam. The 787 heats its wing leading edges electrically, trading bleed air for generator power. Research follows icephobic coatings and electro-expulsive systems that shatter ice with a short pulse. Search for "electro-expulsive de-icing" and "icephobic coating".
